claim: Ca2+, cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP), and Protein Kinase A (PKA) exist in an oscillatory circuit in β cells characterized by a high degree of feedback.
source: In β cells, Ca2+, cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP), and Protein Kinase A (PKA) exist in an oscillatory circuit characterized by a high degree of feedback.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known characteristic of β cells.

claim: Nanodomain clustering of Ca2+-sensitive adenylyl cyclases (ACs) drives oscillations of local cAMP levels to be precisely in-phase with Ca2+ oscillations in mouse MIN6 β cells.
source: We show that in mouse MIN6 β cells, nanodomain clustering of Ca2+-sensitive adenylyl cyclases (ACs) drives oscillations of local cAMP levels to be precisely in-phase with Ca2+ oscillations, whereas Ca2+-sensitive phosphodiesterases maintain out-of-phase oscillations outside of the nanodomain.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Ca2+-sensitive phosphodiesterases maintain out-of-phase oscillations outside of the nanodomain.
source: We show that in mouse MIN6 β cells, nanodomain clustering of Ca2+-sensitive adenylyl cyclases (ACs) drives oscillations of local cAMP levels to be precisely in-phase with Ca2+ oscillations, whereas Ca2+-sensitive phosphodiesterases maintain out-of-phase oscillations outside of the nanodomain.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Disruption of the precise phase relationship between cAMP and Ca2+ perturbs Ca2+ oscillations.
source: Disruption of this precise phase relationship perturbs Ca2+ oscillations, suggesting the relative phase within an oscillatory circuit can encode specific functional information.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing effects of phase disruption on Ca2+ oscillations.

claim: The relative phase within an oscillatory circuit can encode specific functional information.
source: Disruption of this precise phase relationship perturbs Ca2+ oscillations, suggesting the relative phase within an oscillatory circuit can encode specific functional information.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that disrupting phase relationships affects Ca2+ oscillations.

claim: cAMP and Ca2+ act as essential second messengers in almost every cell type.
source: Cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) and Ca2+ act as essential second messengers in almost every cell type and regulate many functional pathways within a cell, such as hormonal signal transduction, metabolism, and secretion (Clapham, 2007; Sassone-Corsi, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: cAMP and Ca2+ regulate many functional pathways within a cell, such as hormonal signal transduction, metabolism, and secretion.
source: Cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) and Ca2+ act as essential second messengers in almost every cell type and regulate many functional pathways within a cell, such as hormonal signal transduction, metabolism, and secretion (Clapham, 2007; Sassone-Corsi, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: In neurons, cardiomyocytes, and pancreatic β cells, cAMP and Ca2+ concentrations oscillate intracellularly.
source: In some cell types, including neurons, cardiomyocytes, and pancreatic β cells, these messengers' concentrations oscillate intracellularly (Dupont et al., 2011; Dyachok et al., 2006), and the oscillations encode critical signaling information (e.g. signal strength, duration, and target diversity) into parameters such as frequency and amplitude (Berridge et al., 1998; De Pittà et al., 2008; Parekh, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Oscillations of cAMP and Ca2+ encode critical signaling information into parameters such as frequency and amplitude.
source: In some cell types, including neurons, cardiomyocytes, and pancreatic β cells, these messengers' concentrations oscillate intracellularly (Dupont et al., 2011; Dyachok et al., 2006), and the oscillations encode critical signaling information (e.g. signal strength, duration, and target diversity) into parameters such as frequency and amplitude (Berridge et al., 1998; De Pittà et al., 2008; Parekh, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Oscillations of Ca2+ drive pulsatile insulin secretion in β cells.
source: This phenomenon is perhaps best exemplified in β cells, where oscillations of Ca2+ drive pulsatile insulin secretion (Rorsman and Ashcroft, 2018) and oscillating cAMP levels (Nesher et al., 2002; Tengholm, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Ca2+, cAMP, and PKA constitute a highly coordinated oscillatory circuit responsible for integrating metabolic and signaling information.
source: Furthermore, Ca2+, cAMP, and the downstream cAMP-dependent kinase protein kinase (PKA) constitute a highly coordinated oscillatory circuit responsible for integrating metabolic and signaling information (Ni et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Both Ca2+ and cAMP are highly spatially compartmentalized and form signaling microdomains or nanodomains.
source: Both Ca2+ and cAMP are highly spatially compartmentalized and form signaling microdomains or nanodomains (Calebiro and Maiellaro, 2014; Petersen, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Ca2+ levels are locally controlled by channels, pumps, and intracellular buffering systems.
source: While Ca2+ levels are locally controlled by channels, pumps, and intracellular buffering systems (Clapham, 2007; Stern, 1992), cAMP is thought to be regulated via controlled synthesis by adenylyl cyclases (ACs) and degradation by phosphodiesterases (PDEs) (Bender and Beavo, 2006; Defer et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: cAMP is regulated via controlled synthesis by adenylyl cyclases (ACs) and degradation by phosphodiesterases (PDEs).
source: While Ca2+ levels are locally controlled by channels, pumps, and intracellular buffering systems (Clapham, 2007; Stern, 1992), cAMP is thought to be regulated via controlled synthesis by adenylyl cyclases (ACs) and degradation by phosphodiesterases (PDEs) (Bender and Beavo, 2006; Defer et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The mechanisms that spatially constrain cAMP await to be fully elucidated.
source: Despite extensive studies on cAMP compartmentation, the mechanisms that spatially constrain this mobile second messenger await to be fully elucidated (Saucerman et al., 2014; Lohse et al., 2017; Musheshe et al., 2018; Bock et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: AKAP79/150 organizes a macromolecular complex with binding partners including PKA, CaV1.2, PKC, calcineurin, Ca2+-sensitive ACs, AMPA receptors, and others.
source: In several excitable cell types, the plasma membrane (PM)-localized scaffold protein AKAP79 (rodent ortholog AKAP150) has been shown to organize a macromolecular complex with binding partners that include PKA, the voltage-gated Ca2+ channel CaV1.2, Protein Kinase C (PKC), the Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein phosphatase calcineurin, Ca2+-sensitive ACs, AMPA receptors, and many others (Gold et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Knock-out of AKAP79/150 results in functional impairment of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS) in pancreatic β cells.
source: Due to the extensive and multivalent nature of AKAP79/150 (as the scaffold is commonly referred) and a report describing the functional impairment of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS) in pancreatic β cells upon its knock-out (Hinke et al., 2012), we hypothesized that the AKAP79/150 scaffold might play an important role in the spatiotemporal regulation of the Ca2+-cAMP-PKA oscillatory circuit.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: cAMP oscillations measured within the AKAP79/150 compartment were in-phase with oscillating Ca2+ in MIN6 cells.
source: cAMP oscillations measured within the AKAP79/150 compartment were in-phase with oscillating Ca2+, such that each transient spike in intracellular Ca2+ was closely associated with a transient increase in cAMP (Figure 1c) (n = 60 cells).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: cAMP oscillations measured within the general plasma membrane compartment were out-of-phase with Ca2+ oscillations in MIN6 cells.
source: This was in sharp contrast to cAMP oscillations measured within the general plasma membrane compartment, where each local Ca2+ peak corresponded to a local trough in cAMP (n = 24), followed by a slow reversal of both signals to a pre-stimulated baseline (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Within the AKAP79/150 compartment, cAMP lagged behind Ca2+ by an average of 13 ± 3 s (n = 60).
source: Within the AKAP79/150 compartment, cAMP lagged behind Ca2+ by an average of only 13 ± 3 s (mean ± SEM, n = 60); however, cAMP within the general plasma membrane compartment oscillated with a lag time of 47 ± 4 s (n = 24) behind Ca2+ (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: cAMP within the general plasma membrane compartment oscillated with a lag time of 47 ± 4 s (n = 24) behind Ca2+.
source: Within the AKAP79/150 compartment, cAMP lagged behind Ca2+ by an average of only 13 ± 3 s (mean ± SEM, n = 60); however, cAMP within the general plasma membrane compartment oscillated with a lag time of 47 ± 4 s (n = 24) behind Ca2+ (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: cAMP oscillates with different phases between the cytosol/plasma membrane and the immediate vicinity of AKAP79/150 within the same cell.
source: After stimulating the signaling circuit, we observed anti-correlated cAMP oscillations, indicating that cAMP oscillates with different phases between the cytosol/plasma membrane and the immediate vicinity of AKAP79/150 within the same cell (n = 25) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Acute addition of 8MM-IBMX (100 μM), a relatively selective PDE1 inhibitor, effectively uncoupled cAMP dynamics from Ca2+ oscillations.
source: Indeed, acute addition of 8MM-IBMX (100 μM), a relatively selective PDE1 inhibitor, effectively uncoupled cAMP dynamics from Ca2+ oscillations (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a) (n = 18), indicating that Ca2+-triggered activation of PDE1 mediates the transient cAMP decreases.
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Ca2+-triggered activation of PDE1 mediates the transient cAMP decreases.
source: Indeed, acute addition of 8MM-IBMX (100 μM), a relatively selective PDE1 inhibitor, effectively uncoupled cAMP dynamics from Ca2+ oscillations (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a) (n = 18), indicating that Ca2+-triggered activation of PDE1 mediates the transient cAMP decreases.
evidence: This is inferred from the effect of PDE1 inhibition on cAMP-Ca2+ coupling.

claim: Treating cells with milrinone (PDE3 inhibitor, 10 μM) or rolipram (PDE4 inhibitor, 1 μM) had no effect on cAMP-Ca2+ coupling or relative phase.
source: While treating cells with either milrinone (PDE3 inhibitor, 10 μM, n = 12) or rolipram (PDE4 inhibitor, 1 μM, n = 15) slightly increased cAMP levels, neither inhibitor had an effect on cAMP-Ca2+ coupling or relative phase (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c.

claim: PDE1 is the key component that couples Ca2+ and cAMP oscillations within this signaling circuit.
source: These data suggest that PDE1 is the key component that couples Ca2+ and cAMP oscillations within this signaling circuit.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing PDE1 inhibition uncouples cAMP from Ca2+.

claim: The phase relationship between cAMP and Ca2+ can be tuned by altering the relative strength between Ca2+-sensitive ACs and PDEs.
source: Thus, our simplified model indicates that the phase relationship can be tuned by altering the relative strength between Ca2+-sensitive ACs and PDEs (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a prediction from computational modeling shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Knocking down AC8 in MIN6 cells results in most cells exhibiting out-of-phase cAMP oscillations within the AKAP79/150 compartment (average lag time 37 ± 9 s, n = 11).
source: To test this prediction, we knocked down endogenous AC8 in MIN6 cells as previously done (Raoux et al., 2015) and observed that most cells exhibited out-of-phase cAMP oscillations within the AKAP79/150 compartment (average lag time 37 ± 9 s, n = 11) (Figure 2d), indicating an AC8-specific role in mediating the cAMP-Ca2+ phase signature.
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: AC8 overexpression reversed the out-of-phase cAMP-Ca2+ phase relationship in the general plasma membrane compartment in a titratable manner (average lag time 23 ± 2 s, n = 56).
source: Interestingly, we found that AC8 overexpression reversed the out-of-phase cAMP-Ca2+ phase relationship in a titratable manner, where the percentage of in-phase oscillating cells correlated with increasing amounts of co-transfected AC8 (average lag time 23 ± 2 s, n = 56) (Figure 2e, Figure 2—figure supplement 2a–d).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: AKAP150 molecules are organized in clusters with a mean radius of 127 ± 9 nm and an average nearest-neighbor spacing of 313 ± 20 nm between cluster centers (n = 20).
source: We found that AKAP150 molecules were organized in clusters with a mean radius of 127 ± 9 nm and an average nearest-neighbor spacing of 313 ± 20 nm between cluster centers (n = 20) (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with several recent reports demonstrating AKAP79/150's tendency to form nanoclusters in other cell types (Mo et al., 2017; Purkey et al., 2018; Tajada et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from STORM imaging shown in Figure 3a.

claim: AC8 distributes non-uniformly at the plasma membrane and forms clusters with a mean radius of 88 ± 8 nm and an average nearest-neighbor spacing of 292 ± 16 nm between cluster centers (n = 16).
source: We found AC8 also distributes non-uniformly at the plasma membrane and forms clusters with a mean radius of 88 ± 8 nm and an average nearest-neighbor spacing of 292 ± 16 nm between cluster centers (n = 16) (Figure 3b; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from STORM imaging shown in Figure 3b.

claim: 72% of AKAP150 localizations were co-clustered with AC8 localizations.
source: In order to measure the degree of colocalization between AKAP150 and AC8 nanoclusters, we also performed 2-color STORM and observed 72% of AKAP150 localizations were co-clustered with AC8 localizations, suggesting the presence of AKAP150:AC8 co-clustered nanodomains (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–e).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from 2-color STORM imaging shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: AC8 diffuses slowly at the membrane with an apparent diffusivity of 0.019 ± 0.002 μm2/s and an average immobile fraction of approximately 42.3% (n = 16).
source: Next, to determine the mobility of AC8 molecules within the timescale of the oscillatory circuit's period, we performed Fluorescence Recovery After Photobleaching (FRAP) with EGFP-tagged AC8 and found AC8 diffuses slowly at the membrane, and that there exists a significant immobile fraction (DAC8 = 0.019 ± 0.002 μm2/s, avg. % immobile = 42.3%, n = 16) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from FRAP experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Overexpression of the AC81-106 peptide led to a decrease in the percentage of AC8 single-molecule localizations within AC8 nanoclusters (n = 9).
source: Furthermore, STORM imaging showed that overexpression of the AC81-106 peptide led to a decrease in the percentage of AC8 single-molecule localizations within AC8 nanoclusters (n = 9) (Figure 5a), consistent with the predicted redistribution of AC8 molecules (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by STORM imaging data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Overexpression of AC81-106 resulted in a significant increase in the average lag time between cAMP and Ca2+ at the AKAP79/150 compartment (43 ± 6 s, n = 33).
source: To test the impact of loss of AC8 molecules from the nanoclusters on the oscillation phase, we measured AKAP79/150-localized cAMP in the presence of AC81-106 and observed a significant increase in the average lag time (43 ± 6 s, n = 33) (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Cells expressing the AC81-106 peptide had a 39 ± 4% reduction in PLA signals compared to non-transfected cells.
source: The disruption of the AKAP150:AC8 interaction was validated using a proximity ligation assay (PLA) to visualize the AKAP150:AC8 interaction in situ. Compared to non-transfected cells, cells expressing the AC81-106 peptide had a 39 ± 4% reduction in the PLA signals, indicating a decrease in the AKAP150:AC8 interaction (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from PLA experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: PKA activity oscillates with a lag time of 25 ± 6 s (n = 15) within the AKAP79/150 compartment.
source: Upon TEA stimulation, PKA activity was observed to oscillate with a lag time of 25 ± 6 s (n = 15) within the AKAP79/150 compartment but with a lag time of 55 ± 8 s (n = 12) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b–e) at the general plasma membrane, indicating that the compartmentalized phase relationship is preserved from cAMP to PKA.
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: PKA activity oscillates with a lag time of 55 ± 8 s (n = 12) at the general plasma membrane.
source: Upon TEA stimulation, PKA activity was observed to oscillate with a lag time of 25 ± 6 s (n = 15) within the AKAP79/150 compartment but with a lag time of 55 ± 8 s (n = 12) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b–e) at the general plasma membrane, indicating that the compartmentalized phase relationship is preserved from cAMP to PKA.
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expression of the AC81-106 disruptor peptide was correlated with a significant decrease in the peak ratio between the second Ca2+ peak and the first Ca2+ peak (control average −1.6%, n = 270; AC81-108 average −10.8%, n = 562).
source: Interestingly, we found that the expression of the disruptor peptide was correlated with a significant decrease in the peak ratio between the second Ca2+ peak and the first Ca2+ peak (control average −1.6%, n = 270; AC81-108 average −10.8%, n = 562) post TEA addition, indicative of less sustained oscillations (Figure 6b,c).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 6b,c.

claim: In the presence of the AC81-106 disruptor peptide, cells exhibited a longer elapsed time between oscillatory Ca2+ peaks (control average 3.9 ± 0.1 min, n = 270; AC81-108 average 4.6 ± 0.1 min, n = 562).
source: In the presence of the disruptor peptide, cells also exhibited a longer elapsed time between oscillatory Ca2+ peaks (control average 3.9 ± 0.1 min, n = 270; AC81-108 average 4.6 ± 0.1 min, n = 562), suggesting that the timing of the signaling circuit was disturbed (Figure 6b,c).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 6b,c.

claim: There is a positive correlation between the percentage of cells exhibiting irregular oscillations and the expression level of the AC81-106 disruptor peptide (42% for low-expressing vs. 68% for high-expressing AC81-106 disruptor).
source: By stratifying the disruptor peptide-expressing cell population into 'low, 'medium,' and 'high' expressers and performing a blinded classification of responding cells based on the regularity of the Ca2+ oscillation (see Appendix 1 for details), we found a positive correlation between the percentage of cells exhibiting irregular oscillations and the expression level of the disruptor peptide (42% for low-expressing vs. 68% for high-expressing AC81-106 disruptor) (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: The compartmentalized cAMP-Ca2+ phase relationship regulates the oscillatory Ca2+ signal and plays an important role in determining the pace, regularity, and sustainability of the Ca2+ oscillations.
source: Taken together, these data signify that the compartmentalized cAMP-Ca2+ phase relationship regulates the oscillatory Ca2+ signal and plays an important role in determining the pace, regularity, and sustainability of the Ca2+ oscillations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing effects of phase disruption on Ca2+ oscillation properties.

claim: Human AKAP79 and rodent AKAP150 share only 53% sequence identity overall.
source: Although human AKAP79 and the rodent AKAP150 share only 53% sequence identity overall, the interaction motifs and association between the AKAP scaffold and other key signaling players such as PKA, the voltage-gated calcium channel, adenylyl cyclases, and calcineurin are highly conserved (Willoughby et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about the sequence similarity between AKAP79 and AKAP150.

claim: The interaction motifs and association between the AKAP scaffold and other key signaling players such as PKA, the voltage-gated calcium channel, adenylyl cyclases, and calcineurin are highly conserved between AKAP79 and AKAP150.
source: Although human AKAP79 and the rodent AKAP150 share only 53% sequence identity overall, the interaction motifs and association between the AKAP scaffold and other key signaling players such as PKA, the voltage-gated calcium channel, adenylyl cyclases, and calcineurin are highly conserved (Willoughby et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The functional equivalence of AKAP79 and AKAP150 has been demonstrated in several reciprocal knock-out and recovery experiments.
source: The functional equivalence of AKAP79 and AKAP150 has been demonstrated in several reciprocal knock-out and recovery experiments in which AKAP79 or AKAP150 was knocked out and expression of the other was shown to rescue a measured phenotype (Hoshi et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The phase in an oscillatory signaling circuit represents a novel mode of informational encoding for which the phase itself can be spatiotemporally regulated.
source: Biological oscillations represent a rich way of encoding information using the amplitude and frequency. Here, we show the phase in an oscillatory signaling circuit represents a novel mode of informational encoding for which the phase itself can be spatiotemporally regulated.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings.

claim: Localized perturbation of the spatial phase signature disrupts global Ca2+ oscillations.
source: Localized perturbation of this spatial phase signature disrupts global Ca2+ oscillations and thus has far-reaching consequences on the functional landscape of the β cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data showing effects of phase perturbation.

claim: The generation of local cAMP gradients around single enzymes appears unfeasible given the measured kinetic rates of most ACs and PDEs.
source: Given the measured kinetic rates of most ACs and PDEs, the generation of local cAMP gradients around single enzymes appears unfeasible (Conti et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Context-dependent discrepancies in kinetics and slower cAMP diffusion due to buffering have been shown to be important for cAMP compartmentalization.
source: Context-dependent discrepancies in some of the kinetics (i.e. differences between in vitro and in vivo measurements) and slower cAMP diffusion due to buffering have been shown to be important for cAMP compartmentalization (Bock et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Approximately 15–150 individual AC8 molecules comprise AKAP150:AC8 nanoclusters.
source: According to our rough estimates, approximately 15–150 individual AC8 molecules comprise AKAP150:AC8 nanoclusters (see Materials and methods for STORM-based estimation).
evidence: This is an estimate based on STORM imaging analysis described in the Materials and methods.

claim: Increasing the number of AC8 molecules leads to a reduction of the noise in the cAMP response.
source: Interestingly, we also noted that increasing the number of AC8 molecules leads to a reduction of the noise in the cAMP response. Thus, we predict that tuning AC8 cluster size might be a biological design strategy of nanoclusters to maintain accurate responses to perturbations (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a–d).
evidence: This is a prediction from stochastic simulations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: PKA has been shown to phosphorylate CaV1.2 in an AKAP79/150-dependent manner, and this modification can influence the open probability of the channel.
source: For example, PKA has been shown to phosphorylate CaV1.2 in an AKAP79/150-dependent manner, and this modification can influence the open probability of the channel (Murphy et al., 2014), suggesting a mechanistic link between local cAMP/PKA activity and global oscillatory Ca2+.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Localized cAMP/PKA signaling at the AKAP79/150 scaffold might play a critical role in regulating insulin secretion due to close interactions between AKAP79/150 and insulin secretory granules via CaV1.2.
source: Localized cAMP/PKA signaling at the AKAP79/150 scaffold and the in-phase oscillations of cAMP and Ca2+ within this compartment might play a critical role in regulating insulin secretion due to close interactions between AKAP79/150 and insulin secretory granules via CaV1.2 (Barg et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a speculation based on known interactions, supported by a citation.

claim: PKA-dependent mobilization of granules is an important process in insulin secretion.
source: Several important processes and components of the secretory machinery have been identified as targets of PKA signaling here, such as PKA-dependent mobilization of granules (Renström et al., 1997) and modulation of the synaptosomal protein SNAP25 (Gao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: cAMP has been implicated to play a direct role in fusion pore formation via the cAMP-regulated guanine exchange factor Epac.
source: In addition to PKA-dependent secretory control, cAMP has recently been implicated to play a direct role in fusion pore formation via the cAMP-regulated guanine exchange factor Epac (Guček et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: The nanoscale organization of key cAMP effectors and regulators is a novel mechanism for cAMP compartmentation.
source: Here, we propose the nanoscale organization of key cAMP effectors and regulators as a novel mechanism for cAMP compartmentation.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental and computational findings.

claim: Compartmentalized cAMP can emerge from the clustering of many relatively immobile AC8 enzymes at the membrane and bulk distribution of PDE1 in the cytoplasm.
source: Despite the slow rates measured for individual ACs, we computationally and experimentally describe conditions in which the generation of compartmentalized cAMP can emerge from the clustering of many relatively immobile AC8 enzymes at the membrane and bulk distribution of PDE1 in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by both computational modeling and experimental data.

claim: Alterations to the nanoscale organization of AC8 and PDE1 lead to dysregulated Ca2+ oscillations.
source: Alterations to this nanoscale organization lead to dysregulated Ca2+ oscillations, demonstrating the functional importance of maintaining this organization.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data showing effects of disrupting nanoscale organization.

claim: A cell can translate a global signal (Ca2+) into a compartmentalized signal (cAMP/PKA activity) by local activation and global inhibition.
source: This system also serves as a nanoscale demonstration of how a cell can translate a global signal (Ca2+) into a compartmentalized signal (cAMP/PKA activity) by local activation and global inhibition, a strategy that is likely utilized in many other cellular contexts (Levchenko et al., 2000; Purvis and Lahav, 2013).
evidence: This is a general principle inferred from the study's findings, supported by citations to related work.
